chapter_title: Local Data Storage with Shared Preferences and Files

screens.title: Local Data Storage with Shared Preferences and Files
screens.subtitle: When to use key-value preferences and when to store files on device storage

narration.text: In this lesson we learn two foundational ways Android apps store data locally. First, you will become comfortable using a lightweight key-value store for small settings and flags. Second, you will learn file-based storage for larger or unstructured data such as text files, caches, or media. We will compare internal and external storage, show concrete Kotlin examples for saving and reading both preferences and files, and highlight common mistakes like blocking the UI thread or saving sensitive secrets in plain text. You will see a hands-on note-taking example that demonstrates writing to internal storage, and a short code walkthrough showing how to save a string preference using the asynchronous apply method. This matters because choosing the right storage option keeps your app responsive, secure, and user-friendly. By the end you should be able to pick SharedPreferences or file storage based on data size, privacy requirements, and sharing needs. Think about this question as we start: when is a simple key-value entry enough, and when do you need a file?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Use SharedPreferences for small, private key-value data and internal or external files for larger or shareable content; always avoid blocking the UI thread and protect sensitive data.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Practical skills you will practice and verify

narration.text: These objectives focus on practical competence with local storage. First, you will learn to choose between SharedPreferences and files based on the data's shape and privacy needs. Second, you will implement saving and retrieving key-value data with SharedPreferences, using the recommended asynchronous write method. Third, you will understand the differences between internal and external storage, the permissions model, and where to place temporary versus persistent files. Fourth, you will practice file input and output to internal storage and learn how to handle the common input and output exceptions. Each objective is paired with a practical milestone: for example, you will save a theme preference and load it across restarts, and you will write a text note into internal storage and read it back reliably. These are not theoretical goals; you will write code, run it in the emulator, and verify persistence using the device file explorer. As you work, pay attention to two common misconceptions: that internal files are completely secure from all attackers, and that synchronous writes never affect UI responsiveness. Both require careful handling and often additional security measures.

screens.title: What is SharedPreferences?
screens.subtitle: A lightweight key-value store for small, persistent settings

narration.text: SharedPreferences is a built-in Android A P I for storing small, primitive values as key-value pairs. It supports booleans, floats, ints, longs, strings, and string sets. This storage is persisted across app restarts and device reboots, and when used with the private mode it is accessible only to your application. SharedPreferences is best for user preferences, flags like onboarding completion, and small pieces of state that do not require complex queries. A practical example is storing a user's theme choice and a boolean indicating whether the onboarding completed. To obtain a SharedPreferences instance you can request a named file for shared use across activities or a default preferences file tied to a single activity. A common misconception is that SharedPreferences is suitable for large or structured data; it is not. Storing lists or binary data here is inefficient and can complicate retrieval. Another common pitfall is blocking the UI thread with synchronous writes. Use the asynchronous apply method to write without blocking, and reserve commit for rare cases when you must confirm a write succeeded. As a takeaway, prefer SharedPreferences for small, private configuration values and avoid it for files, images, or large blobs.

keyIdea.title: SharedPreferences in one line
keyIdea.text: A private, persistent key-value store for small primitives—ideal for settings and flags, not for large data.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › What is SharedPreferences?
Definition
SharedPreferences

A simple API for storing small, primitive values in key-value pairs that persist between app restarts.

Uses
Theme choice, onboarding flag, last sync timestamp.
Limitations
Not for large blobs, images, or structured data.
Pitfall
Using synchronous commits can block the UI thread and cause jank.
Concrete example
Save and load a theme preference
// Save preference (conceptual)
val sharedPref = context.getSharedPreferences("user_settings", Context.MODE_PRIVATE)
with(sharedPref.edit()) {
  putString("theme_preference", "dark")
  putBoolean("onboarding_complete", true)
  apply() // asynchronous write
}

// Retrieve preference (conceptual)
val theme = sharedPref.getString("theme_preference", "light") ?: "light"
val seen = sharedPref.getBoolean("onboarding_complete", false)
Key Takeaway

SharedPreferences is the right tool for small, private configuration data. Use apply() to avoid blocking the UI.

screens.title: Saving and Retrieving with SharedPreferences
screens.subtitle: A code walkthrough demonstrating save and load patterns

narration.text: In this walkthrough you will see the typical save and load pattern with SharedPreferences and learn why the asynchronous write is preferred. Obtain a SharedPreferences instance by requesting a named preferences file with private mode or by using an activity-specific default. When saving, call edit() and then put the values you need. Apply writes the changes asynchronously, which keeps the UI responsive. If you require a synchronous confirmation, commit returns a boolean but blocks the thread, which can cause UI jank. On retrieval, always provide sensible defaults for cases where keys are absent. A concrete example is storing a user's theme and an onboarding flag. Use null-safe retrieval for string values to avoid crashes. A common misconception is that apply may lose data often; apply schedules a background write and will complete normally for typical app flows. Use commit only when you must verify success before proceeding. Finally, if multiple components update the same preferences file concurrently, consider design that minimizes race conditions and persist only necessary state. Saving and Retrieving with SharedPreferences means call edit(), set keys, and use apply() for non-blocking writes; always supply defaults on read.. In practical terms, a code walkthrough demonstrating save and load patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Save/load pattern
keyIdea.text: Call edit(), set keys, and use apply() for non-blocking writes; always supply defaults on read.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Saving & Retrieving
Pattern
Edit, put values, apply
  • Get a preferences instance with a name and MODE_PRIVATE to keep data private.
  • Call edit(), use putString/putBoolean, then apply() to write asynchronously.
  • On read, use getString/getBoolean with safe default values to avoid nulls.
Misconception
apply() is unreliable. In practice apply() is fine for most UI-driven saves; use commit only when you must block and check the result.
Code example
// Conceptual Kotlin
fun saveUserSettings(context: Context, theme: String, seen: Boolean) {
  val sharedPref = context.getSharedPreferences("user_settings", Context.MODE_PRIVATE)
  with(sharedPref.edit()) {
    putString("theme_preference", theme)
    putBoolean("onboarding_complete", seen)
    apply()
  }
}

fun loadUserSettings(context: Context): Pair {
  val sharedPref = context.getSharedPreferences("user_settings", Context.MODE_PRIVATE)
  val theme = sharedPref.getString("theme_preference", "light") ?: "light"
  val onboarding = sharedPref.getBoolean("onboarding_complete", false)
  return Pair(theme, onboarding)
}
Key Takeaway

Always perform preference writes with apply() on the UI thread and avoid commit except when you must synchronously confirm a save.

screens.title: Internal Storage: Private Files and Cache
screens.subtitle: Where your app keeps private files and temporary cache

narration.text: Internal storage is the area of the device file system allocated to your app. Files placed here are private to your app, not visible to other apps or the user via standard file managers, and they are removed when the app is uninstalled. There are two common internal directories you will use: the files directory for persistent private content and the cache directory for temporary files that the system may delete when space is low. You do not need special permissions to read and write these locations. Use filesDir for user-generated data that should persist with the app, and cacheDir for temporary downloads, thumbnails, or transient content. A common misconception is that internal storage is impervious to all attack: while more private than external storage, a rooted device or a device breach can expose these files. For truly sensitive data, consider encryption or platform keystore solutions. Finally, always handle exceptions when performing file input and output and perform these operations off the UI thread to prevent freezing the user interface. Internal Storage: Private Files and Cache means internal files are private and removed on uninstall; cache is temporary and may be cleared by the system.. In practical terms, where your app keeps private files and temporary cache. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Internal storage rules
keyIdea.text: Internal files are private and removed on uninstall; cache is temporary and may be cleared by the system.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Internal Storage
Definition
Internal storage

Private, app-specific storage. No extra permissions required; removed when the app is uninstalled.

filesDir
Persistent private files for your app.
cacheDir
Temporary files the system may clear to reclaim space.
Why it matters

Choosing filesDir or cacheDir affects file lifetime, user privacy, and how you handle cleanup. Temporary downloads belong in cache; persistent user content belongs in files.

Common mistake
Storing large user files in SharedPreferences or assuming cache files won't be removed. Use the right directory for your file's expected lifetime.
Key Takeaway

Use filesDir for persistent private data and cacheDir for temporary files that may be reclaimed by the system.

screens.title: Writing and Reading a Text File (Internal Storage)
screens.subtitle: Try-catch, streams, and reliable reads

narration.text: This lesson walks through writing and reading a text file in internal storage with robust error handling. When writing, open the file output in private mode, write bytes, and close the stream safely. Use a try-catch block to handle IO exceptions and log or surface meaningful messages. When reading, open the input stream, wrap it with a buffered reader, and read lines until the end. Also handle the case where the file does not exist by catching the file not found exception and returning a null or default value. Crucially, perform these operations off the main thread to avoid blocking the UI; use coroutines or executors. A concrete example is saving a user's note to my_private_data. txt and then reading it back to display in the UI. A common misconception is that internal file operations never fail—disk can run out of space or file handles can be closed, so always handle exceptions and test for missing files. The closing question: how will you report read failures to the user while keeping the UI responsive? Writing and Reading a Text File (Internal Storage) means always wrap read and write operations in try-catch blocks and perform them off the ui thread; handle the missing-file case gracefully.. In practical terms, try-catch, streams, and reliable reads. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: File I/O principle
keyIdea.text: Always wrap read and write operations in try-catch blocks and perform them off the UI thread; handle the missing-file case gracefully.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › File I/O Example
Write to internal storage
// Conceptual Kotlin
fun writeToFile(context: Context, filename: String, content: String) {
  try {
    context.openFileOutput(filename, Context.MODE_PRIVATE).use {
      it.write(content.toByteArray())
      // file written
    }
  } catch (e: IOException) {
    // handle error
  }
}
Use use() to ensure streams are closed and catch IOExceptions to handle disk or permission errors.
Read from internal storage
// Conceptual Kotlin
fun readFromFile(context: Context, filename: String): String? {
  try {
    context.openFileInput(filename).use { inputStream ->
      val reader = BufferedReader(InputStreamReader(inputStream))
      val sb = StringBuilder()
      var line: String?
      while (reader.readLine().also { line = it } != null) {
        sb.append(line).append("
")
      }
      return sb.toString()
    }
  } catch (e: FileNotFoundException) {
    return null
  } catch (e: IOException) {
    return null
  }
}
Key Takeaway

Use buffered readers, close streams safely, and handle both missing files and IO errors while running on a background thread.

screens.title: Safe File I/O: Threads and Exceptions
screens.subtitle: Keep the UI responsive and handle errors predictably

narration.text: When performing file operations, two operational concerns dominate: threads and exceptions. Never run disk writes or long reads on the UI thread, because blocking operations will freeze the interface and may trigger an ANR. Use Kotlin coroutines, a background executor, or another off-main-thread mechanism to move input and output work off the main thread. Next, always wrap file operations in try-catch blocks to capture FileNotFoundException and general IOExceptions. Return a null or default value when a file is missing and surface a user-friendly message if a read fails. Ensure streams are closed using language constructs that automatically release resources. For writes, consider atomicity: write to a temporary file and move it into place if you need to avoid partial writes. A common misconception is that small files are safe to write on the UI thread; even small writes can stall the UI on slow devices or when many operations occur. Finally, test your app under low storage conditions and simulate permission denial for external storage to ensure graceful failure modes. Safe File I/O: Threads and Exceptions means always perform i/o off the main thread, handle exceptions, and prefer safe write patterns to avoid corrupt files.. In practical terms, keep the ui responsive and handle errors predictably. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: I/O etiquette
keyIdea.text: Always perform I/O off the main thread, handle exceptions, and prefer safe write patterns to avoid corrupt files.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Safe File I/O
Steps
  1. Move file operations to a background thread or coroutine.
  2. Wrap reads and writes in try-catch to handle IO errors.
  3. Close streams with use() or finally blocks to avoid leaks.
  4. Consider temporary files and atomic file replacement for safe writes.
Common mistake
Assuming the UI thread is safe for a few small writes. Test on low-end devices and simulate slow storage.
Concrete example
Use a coroutine with Dispatchers.IO for file I/O and report results back on the main dispatcher to update UI elements like a Toast or an EditText safely.
Key Takeaway

Treat file I/O as a background concern and always handle missing files or IO errors gracefully in UI code.

screens.title: Internal vs External Storage
screens.subtitle: When to keep files private and when to share them

narration.text: Choosing between internal and external storage depends on privacy, sharing, and lifetime requirements. Internal storage is private to your app and is deleted when the app is uninstalled; it requires no special permissions and is suited for sensitive or app-specific files. External storage is public and can be accessed by the user and other apps; it is appropriate for content you want to share or keep after uninstall, like photos. On modern Android, prefer using platform APIs such as MediaStore for media files on external storage and respect the runtime permission model. A common error is writing private user data to external locations without encrypting it first. Also, assume external storage may not always be available or writable; always check state and request permissions where required. For temporary downloads that should be removed when space is needed, use the app cache directory rather than external storage. As a rule of thumb: internal storage for privacy and small persistent files; external for sharing and long-lived public content. Internal vs External Storage means internal = private, no permissions. external = shareable, needs permissions or mediastore and care for availability.. In practical terms, when to keep files private and when to share them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Storage choice rule
keyIdea.text: Internal = private, no permissions. External = shareable, needs permissions or MediaStore and care for availability.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Internal vs External
Internal Storage
Private to the app
  • No runtime permissions required.
  • Files deleted on uninstall.
  • Use for sensitive or app-only data.
External Storage
Public and shareable
  • Accessible by other apps and the user.
  • Requires runtime permissions or use of MediaStore on modern Android.
  • Good for photos or files that should outlive uninstall.
Quick decision guide
Ask: Do I need the file shared or persistent beyond uninstall? If yes, consider external storage and MediaStore; if no, choose internal storage for privacy.

screens.title: Security and Sensitive Data
screens.subtitle: Why you should never store secrets in plain text locally

narration.text: Handling sensitive data locally requires extra care. While internal storage and SharedPreferences are private to your app by default, they are not a perfect defense against determined attackers or rooted devices. Never store passwords, A P I keys, or tokens in plain text inside SharedPreferences or unencrypted files. Instead, use platform security features such as the Android Keystore or encryption libraries to protect sensitive values. If you must cache tokens, minimize their lifetime and rotate them when possible. Remember to follow least-privilege principles for permissions and avoid requesting external storage access unless necessary. A common misconception is that internal storage is equivalent to encryption; it is not. Treat internal storage as private but not secret. For mobile apps in production, treat sensitive values with encryption at rest and in transit, and log only non-sensitive debug details. The guiding question: which pieces of data in your app require cryptographic protection rather than simple file privacy? Security and Sensitive Data means internal privacy is helpful but not enough for secrets — use encryption or keystore for truly sensitive data.. In practical terms, why you should never store secrets in plain text locally. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Security rule
keyIdea.text: Internal privacy is helpful but not enough for secrets — use encryption or keystore for truly sensitive data.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Security
Why it matters
Protect secrets correctly
Internal storage protects from casual access but not from a rooted device. Encryption and platform keystore provide stronger guarantees for sensitive data.
Practical steps
  • Do not store plaintext passwords or long-lived API keys in files or preferences.
  • Use the Android Keystore for keys and encrypt sensitive blobs before writing them.
  • Limit permission requests and keep tokens short-lived.
Check your understanding
If a token must be stored, ask whether it can be short-lived and encrypted, and whether the keystore can manage the encryption key rather than embedding secrets in code or files.

screens.title: Build the Note-Taking App (Starter Guide)
screens.subtitle: A hands-on practice: save and load a note using internal storage

narration.text: Now we walk through building a simple note-taking app that saves a single note to internal storage and loads it back. The starter layout includes an editable multi-line text field and two controls to save and load. In your activity, obtain references to the edit text and handle clicks by calling the write and read functions we practiced earlier. When saving, use openFileOutput in private mode and write the note as bytes inside a try-catch. Show a brief confirmation like a toast on success and handle errors by logging and displaying a friendly message. When loading, attempt to open the file; if it's missing, inform the user rather than crashing. Always run file operations off the UI thread using coroutines or executors and update the UI on the main thread. After implementing, test by saving text, force-closing the app, and then loading again to confirm persistence. When you inspect the device file explorer you will see the file in the app's internal files directory. This lab trains both the mechanics of file input and output and the discipline of defensive error handling.

keyIdea.title: Lab goal
keyIdea.text: Implement save/load for a single note using internal storage, with try-catch and background threading.

screens.title: When to Choose SharedPreferences vs File Storage
screens.subtitle: A decision checklist for common scenarios

narration.text: Making the right storage choice prevents rework. Use SharedPreferences for small, discrete values like a theme name, a boolean flag, or a last-sync timestamp. Prefer internal files when the data is larger than a few kilobytes, when data includes structured content that is inconvenient to fit into key-value pairs, or when you need to store text or binary content like notes or thumbnails. Choose external storage when you need to share files with other apps or preserve them after uninstall; on modern Android, use the media APIs and request runtime permissions where required. A simple checklist is: 1) Is it small primitive state? Choose SharedPreferences. 2) Is it user content or larger binary? Choose files. 3) Must it be shareable or long-lived beyond uninstall? Consider external storage and MediaStore. Avoid the common mistake of storing lists or JSON blobs in SharedPreferences as this complicates updates and can cause performance issues. When in doubt, prefer a file for complex or large data and keep sensitive material encrypted regardless of storage choice. When to Choose SharedPreferences vs File Storage means small config → sharedpreferences. large or binary → internal files. shareable or long-lived → external storage with proper apis and permissions.. In practical terms, a decision checklist for common scenarios. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Decision checklist
keyIdea.text: Small config → SharedPreferences. Large or binary → internal files. Shareable or long-lived → external storage with proper APIs and permissions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Decision Checklist
Is it a single small value?
If yes, use SharedPreferences to keep things simple and fast.
Is it a document or image?
Use internal files for private storage, cache for temporary data, or external if it must be shared.
Does it need encryption?
Treat any secret as requiring encryption or keystore-backed protection, regardless of internal or external location.
Common pitfall
Avoid stuffing complex or large blobs into SharedPreferences. It complicates updates and harms performance. Use files or a database for structured data.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: To conclude, remember three core ideas. First, SharedPreferences provides a simple key-value store for small primitives and app settings—use apply for asynchronous writes. Second, internal storage is private to your app and ideal for private files or cache; external storage is public and requires permission or modern platform APIs for media. Third, always handle file input and output with try-catch and avoid blocking the UI thread by using background threads or coroutines. Also: never keep sensitive secrets in plain text—use encryption or the platform keystore. These practical rules will help you keep apps reliable, responsive, and safer for users. As a quick self-check: can you explain why a theme setting belongs in SharedPreferences and why a user note belongs in internal files? If yes, you are ready to build the lab and verify persistence on a device.

keyIdea.title: Three quick rules
keyIdea.text: Small settings → SharedPreferences. Private files → internal storage. Large/shareable files → external with permissions and MediaStore.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Key Concepts
SharedPreferences
Small primitives and settings stored as key-value pairs. Use apply() for non-blocking writes.
Internal Storage
Private app files and cache. No permissions required; files are removed on uninstall.
External Storage
Use for shareable, long-lived files. Respect runtime permissions or use MediaStore on modern Android.
Final takeaway
Map data characteristics to storage choices, avoid blocking the UI, and protect sensitive data with encryption or keystore-backed storage.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders before you practice

narration.text: Before you code, keep three reminders: prefer SharedPreferences for small configuration values, use internal files for private user content and cache for temporary downloads, and perform all file input and output on background threads with proper exception handling. Protect really sensitive data with encryption or the keystore. These simple rules will prevent common bugs like UI freezes, accidental public exposure of private files, and data loss on uninstall. As you implement the lab, try to explain each choice aloud: why use a preference here, why a file there, and how you will handle errors. That reflection will help you internalize the practice and make better design decisions in future projects. What to Remember means sharedpreferences for small values, internal files for private data, perform i/o off the main thread and handle exceptions.. In practical terms, three compact reminders before you practice. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Three reminders
keyIdea.text: SharedPreferences for small values, internal files for private data, perform I/O off the main thread and handle exceptions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Quick Reminders
